9580:
"Kick the habit" means to stop doing something that you do regularly, especially something that is bad for you or hard to stop.

The "habit" here refers to a repeated behavior that has become so automatic it feels almost impossible to quit. And "kick" means to forcefully get rid of it — not just reduce it, but eliminate it completely.

So when someone says "I finally kicked the habit," they mean: "I permanently stopped doing something that had a strong hold on me."
Breaking It Down Word by Word

Kick — In everyday English, "kick" literally means to strike something with your foot. But here, it is used figuratively (not literally). When you "kick" something in an idiom, you are forcefully pushing it away or getting it out of your life. Think of it like kicking a stone out of your path — you are removing an obstacle with force and intention.

Habit — A habit is something you do so often and so automatically that it becomes part of your routine. Habits can be good (like exercising every morning) or bad (like biting your nails). In this idiom, "habit" almost always refers to a bad habit — something unhealthy, harmful, or difficult to control.
Why "Kick"? Why Not "Stop" or "Quit"?

This is an important question. You could say "stop the habit" or "quit the habit," and people would understand you. But "kick the habit" carries a much stronger emotional weight. Here's why:

The word "kick" suggests that the habit was fighting back — that it was not easy to let go of, that it required real struggle and force. It implies the person had to make a serious effort to break free. So "kick the habit" doesn't just mean stopping something. It means overcoming something that had power over you.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The origin of "kick the habit" is closely tied to the world of drug addiction.

The word "habit" has long been used as a slang term for drug addiction, especially in American English from the early 20th century. Someone who was addicted to drugs was said to "have a habit." The phrase "kick the habit" emerged from this context, meaning to break free from a drug addiction — which, as anyone can imagine, requires enormous willpower and pain.

Over time, the phrase moved beyond drug addiction and entered everyday language. Today, people use it for all kinds of bad habits, not just addiction to substances.
How and When to Use It

"Kick the habit" is used in informal, everyday conversation. It is not formal or academic language. You would say it when talking to friends, family, or in casual writing — not in a formal essay or business report.

It is used when:

  • Someone has finally stopped a long-standing bad behavior.
  • Someone is trying to stop or is planning to stop a bad behavior.
  • Someone is encouraging another person to stop a bad behavior.
Real-Life Examples

Here are examples showing how the idiom works in different situations:

Smoking:
"My uncle smoked for 20 years, but he finally kicked the habit after his doctor warned him."
→ He permanently stopped smoking after struggling with it for a long time.

Social media addiction:
"I was on my phone for 6 hours every day. It took me three months, but I kicked the habit."
→ The speaker worked hard and succeeded in stopping their excessive phone use.

Eating junk food:
"She used to eat chips every night before bed, but she's trying to kick the habit."
→ She has not fully quit yet, but she is making an effort to stop.

Encouraging someone:
"You should really kick the habit of staying up until 3 AM. It's ruining your health."
→ The speaker is advising someone to stop a harmful behavior.

Biting nails:
"I've been biting my nails since I was a child. I just can't seem to kick the habit."
→ The person has tried to stop but finds it very difficult.
Important Grammar Notes

"Kick the habit" uses "the" — not "a."

You say: "kick the habit" ✅
You don't say: "kick a habit" ❌ (This sounds unnatural in this idiom.)

The "the" suggests a specific habit — the one this particular person struggles with.

It works in all tenses:

  • Past: "She kicked the habit."
  • Present: "He is trying to kick the habit."
  • Future: "I will kick the habit someday."
  • Perfect: "They have finally kicked the habit."
Variations of This Idiom

You may also hear these similar expressions that carry nearly the same meaning:

"Break the habit" — Very common and almost identical in meaning. Slightly softer in tone than "kick." "I'm trying to break the habit of checking my email at midnight."

"Shake the habit" — Less common, but used occasionally. It implies the habit clings to you like something you're trying to shake off. "He just couldn't shake the habit."

"Quit the habit" — Straightforward and direct. Less colorful than "kick." "She finally quit the habit of oversleeping."

Among all these, "kick the habit" is the most energetic and expressive, which is why it remains the most popular.
What This Idiom Does NOT Mean

To be completely clear, here is what "kick the habit" does not mean:

❌ It does not mean to reduce the habit. It means to completely stop it.
❌ It does not mean to take a short break from something. It implies a permanent or long-term change.
❌ It does not always refer to drug addiction anymore. In modern usage, it applies to any bad habit.
The Feeling Behind the Idiom

When someone says they "kicked the habit," there is often a sense of pride, relief, and accomplishment in those words. It acknowledges that quitting was hard — that the habit had real power — but that the person won. It is a small celebration of personal strength.

This emotional depth is what makes "kick the habit" such a lasting and beloved phrase in the English language.
Quick Summary

MeaningTo permanently stop a bad, addictive, or hard-to-break habit
ToneInformal, conversational
StrengthImplies the habit was powerful and required real effort to overcome
OriginSlang from drug addiction culture, now used broadly
Used forSmoking, drinking, junk food, social media, nail-biting, and any repeated bad behavior
9581:
To kick up a fuss means to complain loudly, protest strongly, or make a big scene about something — often in a way that seems excessive or unnecessary to the people around you. When someone kicks up a fuss, they are expressing their anger, displeasure, or disagreement in a very loud, dramatic, or persistent way.

Think of it this way: imagine a child in a supermarket who does not want to leave. They start crying, shouting, and stomping their feet. That child is "kicking up a fuss." Now imagine an adult doing something similar — maybe angrily demanding to speak to a manager, loudly complaining about a rule, or causing a scene in public. That is also "kicking up a fuss."

The key idea is that the reaction is bigger, louder, or more dramatic than the situation perhaps deserves. The person is not just quietly unhappy — they are making sure everyone around them knows about it.

Understanding the two parts of this idiom helps it stick in your memory.

"Kick up" is a phrasal verb that means to cause something to happen or to stir something up. You can "kick up dust" (cause dust to fly into the air), "kick up trouble" (cause trouble), or "kick up a storm" (cause a big commotion). In all these cases, "kick up" means you are creating or starting something — usually something disruptive.

"A fuss" means unnecessary noise, excitement, or commotion, especially over something minor. A "fuss" is not calm, quiet, or dignified. It is noisy, agitated, and often emotional. The word "fuss" by itself implies that the reaction is a bit over the top.

So when you put them together: to kick up a fuss = to actively create a loud, dramatic, unnecessary commotion, usually because you are unhappy about something.
The Tone and Feel of This Idiom

This is a very important thing to understand. The idiom carries a slightly negative or dismissive tone. When you say someone "kicked up a fuss," you are subtly suggesting that their reaction was:

  • Too dramatic for the situation
  • Unnecessary or over the top
  • Annoying or inconvenient to others

For example, if your friend got a slightly cold cup of coffee and complained to the waiter, the manager, and wrote an angry review online, you might say, "He kicked up such a fuss over a cup of coffee." You are not saying he was completely wrong to be unhappy — you are saying his reaction was bigger than it needed to be.

However, this tone is not always there. Sometimes, "kick up a fuss" can be used in a neutral or even positive way — especially when someone should complain and refuses to stay silent. For example: "You paid for a service that was never delivered. You should kick up a fuss." Here, the person is being encouraged to stand up for themselves.

So the meaning stays the same, but whether it sounds negative or positive depends on who is kicking up the fuss, why, and whether the speaker thinks they are right to do so.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples that show the idiom in different situations so you can see how naturally it fits into everyday speech.

At a restaurant:
"The customer kicked up a fuss when the waiter brought the wrong dish."
(He complained loudly and made a scene.)

At work:
"She kicked up a fuss about the new office policy, and the manager eventually agreed to change it."
(She protested strongly and persistently until something changed.)

At home:
"The kids kicked up a fuss when their mother said it was bedtime."
(The children cried, argued, and protested dramatically.)

About a small matter:
"He kicked up a huge fuss just because someone parked in 'his' spot."
(His reaction was disproportionately dramatic over something minor.)

Encouraging someone to speak up:
"If the airline loses your luggage, don't just accept it — kick up a fuss and demand compensation."
(Assert yourself loudly and clearly.)

The idiom has a few close relatives that you will encounter in English. They all mean roughly the same thing:

"Make a fuss" — This is the most common and interchangeable variation. "She made a fuss about the noise" means exactly the same as "she kicked up a fuss about the noise." The only tiny difference is that "kick up a fuss" feels slightly more energetic and dramatic than "make a fuss."

"Kick up a stink" — This is a ruder, more informal version. "Stink" adds the idea that the complaint is particularly unpleasant or embarrassing. It is used more in British English.

"Kick up a storm" — This means to cause a very large and intense commotion, bigger than a typical fuss. If "kick up a fuss" is a protest, "kick up a storm" is an uproar.

"Raise a stink" — Similar to kick up a stink; informal and mildly rude.

"Make a scene" — This specifically means causing a public, embarrassing commotion in front of others.

All of these sit in the same family, but "kick up a fuss" is the most commonly used and the most neutral of the group.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The word "fuss" has been in the English language since at least the early 1700s. It originally described a person who was needlessly busy, anxious, or agitated about small things. Over time, it came to describe the noisy commotion itself.

The phrase "kick up" has long been used in English to mean "to cause" or "to stir up" — much like physically kicking something causes it to rise or scatter. Sailors and soldiers historically used "kick up a row" or "kick up a shindy" to describe making a loud disturbance.

"Kick up a fuss" is particularly common in British English, though it is widely understood and used in American English, Australian English, and beyond. If you are watching a British TV show or reading a British novel and someone says this, you will know exactly what they mean.
Register: When and Where Is It Used?

This is an informal idiom. It belongs in casual, everyday conversation — with friends, family, or in informal writing. You would not say "kick up a fuss" in a formal essay, a business report, or an official complaint letter. In those settings, you would instead say something like "lodged a formal complaint," "expressed strong dissatisfaction," or "objected vigorously."

However, it is perfectly normal in:

  • Casual conversation
  • Newspaper articles (especially in British tabloids)
  • Novels and storytelling
  • TV shows and films
  • Text messages and informal emails
The Most Important Thing to Remember

If you want to remember just one thing about this idiom, remember this: someone who kicks up a fuss is not staying quiet. They are upset, and they want everyone to know it — loudly, dramatically, and persistently. Whether that is admirable or annoying depends entirely on the situation.
9582:
To "kick yourself" means to feel deep frustration, regret, or anger directed at yourself because you made a mistake, missed an opportunity, or did something foolish that you clearly could have avoided.

It is the feeling of "I should have known better!" or "Why did I do that?!"

Literally, kicking yourself means physically hitting your own body with your foot — which is painful and makes no real sense to do. That's exactly the point. The idiom captures the idea that your regret is so strong, it feels like you want to punish yourself physically. Of course, nobody actually does this — it is purely an expression of intense self-blame.

Think of a time when you did something — or didn't do something — and immediately thought, "That was such an obvious mistake. I knew better. How did I let this happen?"

That sharp, sinking, self-directed frustration? That is exactly what "kick yourself" describes.

It is not just mild disappointment. It is the kind of regret that stings — especially because the mistake or missed chance feels preventable in hindsight.

1. It is always about regret you feel toward yourself.
You don't kick someone else — you kick yourself. The blame, frustration, and disappointment are all pointed inward, at your own actions or decisions.

2. The regret is usually about something avoidable.
The pain of "kicking yourself" is strongest when you realize the mistake was unnecessary. You had the information, the chance, or the ability — but you still got it wrong or let it slip away.

3. It can be about action OR inaction.
You can kick yourself for doing something wrong, and you can kick yourself for failing to do something you should have done.

The idiom is most commonly used in these patterns:

  • "You'll kick yourself" — a warning that someone will regret something
  • "I could kick myself" — expressing current regret
  • "I kicked myself" — describing past regret
  • "He/she kicked himself/herself" — describing someone else's regret

Example 1:

"I could kick myself — I had tickets to that concert but I sold them, and it turned out to be the best show of the year."

→ The person sold their tickets thinking it wasn't a big deal. Later, they realized it was a huge mistake. The regret is strong because they had the opportunity right in their hands and gave it away.

Example 2:

"You'll kick yourself if you don't apply for that job. You're perfectly qualified."

→ Here, someone is warning a friend. They're saying: "If you let this chance go, you are going to deeply regret it later." It's used as a push or motivation.

Example 3:

"She kicked herself for not buying that house when the price was low. Now it costs twice as much."

→ She had the chance to buy at a good price but didn't. Now she has to live with that decision. The regret is sharp because the answer was obvious in hindsight.

Example 4:

"I kicked myself when I realized I had the answer all along but wrote something completely different."

→ The person had the right knowledge but still made the wrong choice. That kind of self-inflicted mistake produces exactly this type of regret.

Example 5:

"Don't let this sale end without buying — you'll kick yourself tomorrow."

→ A warning that inaction (not buying) will lead to strong regret when the opportunity is gone.

You will hear "kick yourself" in everyday spoken English and informal writing. It appears in:

  • Personal conversations — when someone shares their regret with a friend
  • Advice or warnings — to encourage someone not to miss an opportunity
  • Storytelling — when someone describes a past mistake
  • Sales and marketing language — "You'll kick yourself if you miss this deal!"

It is informal in tone. You would use it comfortably with friends, family, and colleagues in casual settings. In a very formal written document (like a legal report or academic paper), you would instead write something like "deeply regret" or "reproach oneself."
The Difference Between "Kick Yourself" and Simple Regret

Normal regret: "I wish I had done that." — mild, calm disappointment.

Kicking yourself: "I CANNOT BELIEVE I didn't do that. I knew better. How could I?!" — sharp, stinging, self-directed frustration.

The idiom carries more emotional intensity than simply saying "I regret it." It suggests the mistake felt avoidable and obvious, which makes the regret hurt more.

"Kick yourself" vs. "Bite your tongue"
These are different. "Bite your tongue" means stopping yourself from saying something. "Kick yourself" is about regretting a past action or decision — it has nothing to do with speech specifically.

"Kick yourself" vs. "Shoot yourself in the foot"
"Shooting yourself in the foot" means accidentally harming your own chances or situation through your own actions. It's similar but focuses more on accidentally sabotaging yourself, while "kick yourself" focuses more on the emotional regret you feel afterward.

The idiom comes from the visual image of someone being so frustrated with themselves that they want to physically kick their own body as a form of self-punishment. Since you truly can't kick yourself effectively (try it — it's nearly impossible!), the phrase emphasizes just how irrational and overwhelming the feeling of self-blame can be. Language borrowed this physical image to express a powerful emotional experience.

ConceptDetail
Core meaningFeeling strong regret or frustration at yourself for a mistake or missed opportunity
Emotional toneIntense, stinging self-blame — stronger than simple regret
FormalityInformal / everyday English
Used forPast mistakes, missed chances, avoidable errors
Key triggerThe feeling that the mistake was preventable

The next time you hear someone say "I could kick myself," you'll know immediately: they're not talking about any physical action. They're expressing that sharp, painful frustration of realizing they made a mistake they really should have avoided — and they wish, more than anything, they could go back and do it differently.
9583: The word kickback has two completely separate meanings — one involving money and corruption, and one involving physical force. Both are widely used, so you need to understand both. The financial/corruption meaning is by far the more common and important one.

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in news, business, law, and everyday conversation.

A kickback is a sum of money secretly paid to a person in return for helping someone else get a business deal, contract, job, or other benefit — especially when that help involves the person abusing their position of power or trust.

A simple way to picture it

Imagine a government official whose job is to decide which construction company gets a big contract to build a new highway. Company A really wants that contract. So instead of competing fairly, they secretly hand the official a large amount of money "under the table." In exchange, the official makes sure Company A gets selected. That secret payment is the kickback.

The logic of the word makes intuitive sense: a portion of the money from the deal gets "kicked back" to the person who made the deal happen in the first place.

The essential characteristics of a kickback

A kickback is always secret. If the payment were openly declared, it would just be a commission or a fee. The secrecy is what makes it a kickback.

A kickback is almost always illegal. It is treated as a form of bribery and corruption in most countries. Both the person who pays the kickback and the person who receives it are typically committing a crime.

A kickback involves a person in a position of power. The receiver of the kickback is usually someone who has the authority to make a decision that benefits the payer — awarding a contract, approving a purchase, granting a license, choosing a supplier, etc.

A kickback usually involves a percentage of the deal's value. If a supplier wins a $1 million government contract and secretly gives the approving official $100,000, that $100,000 is the kickback — effectively 10% of the deal "kicked back" to the decision-maker.

Common places where kickbacks happen

Kickbacks are most associated with government and public contracting (officials who award public projects), healthcare (doctors or hospital administrators paid by pharmaceutical or medical equipment companies to prefer their products), corporate procurement (a company's purchasing manager secretly paid by a vendor to keep buying from them), and construction and real estate. Anywhere that someone has the power to steer a decision toward a specific party, kickback schemes can exist.

Example sentences

  • "The senator was charged with accepting kickbacks from defense contractors."
  • "The hospital's procurement officer had been receiving kickbacks from a medical supply company for years."
  • "Three executives were fired after an audit uncovered a kickback scheme involving their main supplier."
Meaning 2: A Sudden, Violent Backward Jolt from a Machine

This meaning is entirely physical and has nothing to do with money. A kickback here refers to the sudden, forceful, and often dangerous backward movement that a machine, tool, or firearm produces — usually unexpectedly — during operation.

A simple way to picture it

Imagine you are cutting a log with a chainsaw. If the tip of the blade catches the wood at the wrong angle, the saw can instantly and violently snap back toward your face or body. That dangerous, uncontrolled backward lunge is a kickback.

This meaning is especially important in the context of power tools (chainsaws, circular saws, table saws), where kickback is one of the leading causes of serious injury. It is also used for firearms, where the gun pushes sharply backward against the shooter's hands or shoulder when fired (though for guns, the word "recoil" is more commonly used). The word also applies to engines and other heavy machinery.

Example sentences

  • "The woodworker's hand was severely injured by a kickback from the table saw."
  • "Always wear protective gear and maintain a firm grip to prevent chainsaw kickback."
  • "Kickback injuries from power tools send thousands of people to the emergency room every year."
A Less Common, More Neutral Financial Use

Occasionally, you will hear "kickback" used in a relatively neutral financial sense to mean a portion of money returned to someone as part of a business arrangement — similar to a rebate or a commission.

For example: "Sales agents earn a kickback of 5% on every deal they close."

However, even in this neutral use, the word "kickback" carries a slightly informal and suspicious tone. In professional or formal writing, people prefer cleaner words like commission, rebate, or incentive. Whenever you see "kickback" in a financial context, there is almost always at least a hint of something shady being implied, even if not stated outright.
How to Tell the Two Main Meanings Apart

Context makes it almost impossible to confuse them:

If the sentence involves money, business, government, contracts, or corruption → it is the bribery/illegal payment meaning.

If the sentence involves a tool, a machine, a weapon, or a physical action → it is the sudden backward jolt meaning.

Kickback as a noun has two core meanings:

The primary and most important meaning is a secret, illegal payment made to a person in a position of power in exchange for a favorable decision — a form of bribery and corruption used to rig business deals, contracts, and more. Both giving and receiving kickbacks is typically a crime.

The secondary meaning is a sudden, violent, and dangerous backward recoil produced by a power tool, machine, or firearm during operation — a major safety hazard in settings like woodworking, construction, and forestry.

A third, minor use exists in neutral business language to mean a financial return or commission, but this use is informal and always carries an undercurrent of suspicion.
9584:
To kidnap someone means to take a person away by force, threat, or trickery — against their will — and hold them captive, usually to demand something in return for releasing them.

The person who does this is called a kidnapper. The person taken is called the victim or sometimes the hostage. The act itself is called kidnapping (or a kidnapping).
Breaking It Down: What Must Happen for It to Be Kidnapping

Three things must happen together:

  1. Taking — the kidnapper physically removes the person from where they are, or prevents them from leaving a place freely.
  2. Against the person's will — the victim has not agreed. They do not want to go or stay. They are not free to leave.
  3. By force, threat, or deception — the kidnapper may physically grab them, threaten to hurt them (or someone they love), or trick them into going somewhere.

All three elements work together. If someone willingly goes somewhere with a person and willingly stays — that is not kidnapping.
Who Can Be Kidnapped?

Anyone — a child, a teenager, or a fully grown adult. The word applies regardless of age, gender, or background. A powerful politician can be kidnapped. So can an ordinary person walking down the street. There are no restrictions on who qualifies as a victim.
Why Do Kidnappers Do It? (Motives)

Understanding the motive helps you understand the word more deeply:

  • Ransom — The most common motive. The kidnapper holds the person and demands money from the victim's family, employer, or government. The message is: "Pay us, and we will release them. Don't pay, and they will be harmed."
  • Political demands — A kidnapper (often a terrorist group) may demand that a government release prisoners, change a policy, or make a public statement, in exchange for the hostage.
  • Personal revenge or grudge — Kidnapping someone to punish them or to force them to do something.
  • Human trafficking — People are kidnapped to be sold, exploited for labor, or forced into other criminal activities. This is one of the most severe forms.
  • Custody disputes — A parent who is legally not allowed to take their child away sometimes takes the child anyway, hiding them from the other parent. This is called parental kidnapping (or parental abduction) and is still a crime even though a parent is involved.
How Is It Done?

Kidnappers use different methods:

  • Physical force — grabbing someone, dragging them into a vehicle, restraining them.
  • Threats — "Come with me or I will hurt your child."
  • Deception — "Your mother is in the hospital — I'll take you to her" (a lie, used to lure the person).
  • Drugging — giving the person a substance that makes them unable to resist or stay alert.
What Happens to the Victim During a Kidnapping?

The victim is usually:

  • Kept in a hidden location (a locked room, a remote house, a car trunk)
  • Prevented from contacting anyone
  • Watched constantly so they cannot escape
  • Sometimes tied up, blindfolded, or otherwise restrained
  • Threatened to ensure cooperation

The period of being held like this is called captivity or being held hostage.
Important Distinctions

Kidnapping vs. Arresting someone — Police officers can legally detain and take a person away. That is not kidnapping, because it is authorised by law and follows legal procedures. Kidnapping is always illegal.

Kidnapping vs. Simply locking someone in a room — If someone is trapped against their will but not moved from where they are, that is called false imprisonment or unlawful confinement, not strictly kidnapping. Kidnapping typically involves moving the person somewhere, though in everyday usage people sometimes use the words interchangeably.

Kidnapping vs. Abduction — In everyday English, "abduct" and "kidnap" are used almost synonymously. Technically, "abduction" often refers to the act of taking someone away (the removal itself), while "kidnapping" tends to emphasise both the taking and the holding for a demand. In practice, both words are widely understood to mean the same crime.
The Legal Weight

Kidnapping is a serious crime in every country. It is not a minor offence. Courts treat it severely because it involves depriving a human being of their freedom, causing them fear and trauma, and often threatening their life. A kidnapper can spend many years — sometimes decades — in prison.
How to Use the Word in Sentences

• The criminals kidnapped the businessman and demanded five million dollars for his release.
  • She was kidnapped from outside her school and was found three days later.
  • The government refused to negotiate with those who had kidnapped its ambassador.
  • He was charged with kidnapping after taking his ex-wife's child across the border without permission.
  • The kidnapping was resolved peacefully when the ransom was paid.
Common Word Forms

FormExample
kidnap (base verb)They plan to kidnap him.
kidnapped (past tense / past participle)She was kidnapped last night.
kidnapping (present participle / noun)The kidnapping shocked the nation.
kidnapper (the person who does it)The kidnapper demanded $1 million.
kidnappers (plural)The kidnappers called with demands.
The One-Sentence Summary

To kidnap is to illegally seize a person against their will — using force, threat, or trickery — hold them captive, and typically demand something (money, political concessions, or other favours) in exchange for their freedom.
9585:
A kill switch is a mechanism — a button, lever, feature, or system — that is specifically designed to immediately and completely shut something down, usually in an emergency or as a safety measure. The moment it is activated, whatever it controls stops working — instantly, with no gradual process.

Think of it as a last-resort "stop everything, right now" tool.

The word "kill" here doesn't mean to cause death. It means to terminate or cut off — just like how you might say "kill the lights" to mean "turn the lights off."

A kill switch exists for one primary reason: control in a critical moment.

In many situations, you can't afford to go through a normal shutdown process — it's too slow, too complicated, or too risky. You need something that works immediately, without any extra steps. That's exactly what a kill switch does.

It is almost always:

  • Separate from the normal controls of a system
  • Simple to activate (one press, one flip, one click)
  • Absolute in effect — it doesn't pause or slow things down; it stops them completely

Kill switches are used in many different fields. Understanding all of them will give you a complete picture of the word.

1. Physical Machines (The Original Use)

This is where the idea of a kill switch began. Imagine a large factory machine — a conveyor belt, a wood cutter, or a press. If a worker's hand gets caught in it, there's no time to navigate menus or find the right setting. A large red button — the kill switch — is placed somewhere easy to reach. One press, and the entire machine stops dead.

You see this in everyday life too. Many treadmills come with a small magnetic clip that you attach to your clothing. If you fall and move away from the machine, the clip pulls out and acts as a kill switch — the treadmill stops immediately.

2. Smartphones and Devices

Modern smartphones often have a kill switch feature that lets you remotely disable or wipe your phone if it is lost or stolen. Even if the thief has your phone in their hands, you can activate the kill switch from another device, and your phone becomes completely locked or erased. The thief gets nothing useful.

This type of kill switch is about security rather than physical safety.

3. Software and the Internet

Software programs — especially malicious ones — can also have kill switches built into them. A famous real-world example: in 2017, a dangerous cyberattack called WannaCry was spreading rapidly across the internet, infecting hundreds of thousands of computers worldwide. A security researcher discovered that the attack program was secretly checking a specific website address. If that website was active, the malware would stop running. The researcher registered that web address, and the attack halted almost instantly. That website address acted as the kill switch — a hidden "off" condition baked into the program.

Kill switches can also be built intentionally into legitimate software by companies — to shut down a product remotely if it's being misused, if a critical bug is found, or if a service needs to be terminated.

4. Artificial Intelligence (AI)

As AI systems become more powerful, researchers and developers talk seriously about the need for kill switches for AI. If an AI system starts behaving in unexpected, dangerous, or uncontrollable ways, there must be a way for humans to immediately shut it down before it causes harm. This is considered a critical safety feature in AI development. The idea is that no matter how advanced an AI becomes, humans must always retain the ability to turn it off.

5. Vehicles

Some vehicles — especially those used in racing, or electric vehicles and motorcycles — are fitted with kill switches that cut power to the engine instantly. If a motorcycle rider falls off, the kill switch can prevent the riderless bike from continuing to accelerate. Some modern cars with remote features also allow owners or manufacturers to remotely disable the engine — for example, if a car is reported stolen.

6. Government and the Internet

The term "internet kill switch" refers to a government's ability to shut down internet access across an entire country. Some governments have done this during political unrest or crises to prevent communication and the spread of information. This is a controversial use of the concept, but it perfectly illustrates the idea: one action, taken at the top level, that cuts off an entire system for everyone beneath it.

7. Business and Legal Agreements

In the world of business and contracts, a kill switch can refer to a clause or provision that allows one party to immediately terminate a deal, partnership, or agreement under specific conditions. For example, an investor might have a kill switch in a contract that lets them pull out of a deal instantly if certain financial targets are not met.
Kill Switch vs. a Regular Off Switch — What's the Difference?

This is an important distinction. An ordinary off switch is part of the normal operation of a device. You use it every day. It's routine.

A kill switch is different in three key ways:

  • It's for emergencies or special circumstances, not everyday use
  • It overrides everything — it doesn't care what the system is currently doing; it just stops it
  • It's often a last resort — you reach for it when normal controls have failed or when there's no time for them

Think of a car's ignition button as the regular off switch. But if the car's brakes fail and it's speeding out of control, a kill switch would be a separate mechanism that cuts the engine immediately, regardless of anything else happening.

Because the concept is so powerful and clear, people also use "kill switch" figuratively to describe anything that can instantly end, neutralize, or shut down something — even in non-technical conversations.

For example:

  • "Public outrage was the kill switch for that policy." (Meaning: public anger immediately ended the policy)
  • "The CEO had a kill switch on the entire project." (Meaning: the CEO had the sole power to cancel it at any moment)

A kill switch is a dedicated mechanism — physical or digital — that immediately shuts down or disables a system, machine, process, or operation, typically for safety, security, or emergency reasons. It is designed for speed and certainty: one action, total stop. It exists across machinery, technology, AI, vehicles, governments, and business, and in every context, the core idea remains the same — absolute power to stop something, instantly, when it matters most.
9586: A killjoy is a person who spoils or ruins the fun, happiness, or excitement that others are experiencing. When people around them are enjoying themselves, a killjoy does or says something that brings that good feeling down — like popping a balloon at a party.
The word itself is beautifully self-explanatory: it literally means someone who kills joy — that is, they destroy or extinguish the happiness of a moment or a group.
What Does a Killjoy Actually Do?

A killjoy doesn't necessarily intend to be unpleasant. Sometimes they genuinely believe they are being helpful, responsible, or honest. But the result is the same — they drain the energy and enthusiasm out of a happy situation.

Here are the most common things a killjoy does:

Complains when others are having fun. Everyone is laughing and dancing, and the killjoy stands in the corner saying the music is too loud, the food is bad, or the whole event is a waste of money.

Points out problems when people are excited. Your friend is thrilled about their new car, and the killjoy immediately says, "Cars are terrible for the environment" or "Maintenance costs are going to destroy you."

Gives unwanted warnings or lectures. People are enjoying a meal at a restaurant, and the killjoy starts talking about calories, unhealthy ingredients, or bad hygiene in kitchens.

Refuses to participate and makes it obvious. A killjoy doesn't just quietly step aside from the fun — they make their disapproval visible, which affects everyone else's mood.
The Key Nuance: Intention Doesn't Matter

This is important: a killjoy does not have to mean to ruin the fun. A well-meaning parent who warns their teenager about every possible danger on a school trip is still being a killjoy, even if they're acting out of love. The label focuses on the effect on others, not the intention behind the behaviour.

However, some killjoys are deliberately trying to dampen others' happiness — out of jealousy, bitterness, disapproval, or a need to feel morally superior.

• "We were all so excited about the concert, but David had to be a killjoy and remind us how overpriced the tickets were."
  • "Don't be such a killjoy — let the kids eat the birthday cake without a nutrition lecture."
  • "She's a real killjoy at parties. Every time someone is having a good time, she finds something to criticise."
  • "I know I sound like a killjoy, but we really should head home before the storm hits." (Here, the speaker is gently acknowledging that their own sensible suggestion might dampen the mood.)

Killjoy is an informal word. You'd say it in everyday conversation, not in a formal essay or a legal document.

Calling someone a killjoy is almost always a mild criticism or insult — it means you find their attitude unnecessarily negative or restrictive. However, it is not a deeply harsh insult. It's more of a frustrated, eye-rolling kind of remark. Sometimes, people even use it affectionately or humorously about themselves, as seen in the fourth example above.
Words That Mean the Same Thing

English has several words and phrases that overlap with killjoy. Knowing them will sharpen your understanding:

  • Spoilsport — someone who ruins a game or fun activity, often by refusing to play along or by breaking the mood. Very similar to killjoy.
  • Wet blanket — a person who dampens enthusiasm; the image is of throwing a wet blanket on a fire to put it out.
  • Buzzkill — very informal and modern; someone or something that kills the excitement or "buzz" of a moment.
  • Party pooper — informal; someone who refuses to join in the fun at a social gathering or celebration.

All of these point to the same core idea as killjoy. The differences are very small and mostly about context or degree of formality.

It helps to know what doesn't qualify:

  • Simply being a quiet or introverted person doesn't make someone a killjoy. A killjoy actively interferes with others' fun.
  • Being serious or disciplined in your own life is not being a killjoy. The key is that a killjoy affects other people's joy, not just their own.
  • A person who genuinely and successfully stops a danger (say, pulling a friend back from a real risk) is not a killjoy, even if it ruins the moment — though others might unfairly call them one in the heat of the moment.

A killjoy is someone — intentionally or not — who takes a happy, exciting, or fun moment and makes it smaller, duller, or less enjoyable for everyone else. The word carries a tone of mild frustration and is usually used to criticise someone for being unnecessarily negative, preachy, or cheerless in a moment that calls for enjoyment.

A kiln is a special type of extremely high-temperature oven — not for cooking food, but for transforming raw materials (like clay or stone) into something harder, stronger, or chemically different. Think of it as an industrial or craft furnace that uses intense, controlled heat to permanently change the things placed inside it.

A regular kitchen oven reaches about 250°C (480°F). A kiln can reach 1,400°C (2,550°F) or more — temperatures far beyond what any normal oven could ever achieve. That extreme heat is precisely what makes a kiln powerful and unique.

Kilns come in many shapes and sizes. A small kiln used by an artist in their studio might look like a thick-walled metal box (roughly the size of a mini-fridge), lined on the inside with special heat-resistant bricks or fibre. A large industrial kiln used in a factory can be a massive structure — sometimes a long rotating cylinder or a tunnel hundreds of metres long. Despite the size difference, they all share the same basic idea: a sealed or semi-sealed chamber that can be heated to very high temperatures in a controlled way.
What a Kiln Is Used For

This is where kilns become really interesting, because they serve several very different purposes across different industries.

1. Pottery and Ceramics
This is the most widely known use of a kiln. When a potter shapes a bowl, a mug, or a vase out of clay, that clay object is still soft and fragile — it would crumble if you put water in it. Placing it in a kiln and heating it to very high temperatures causes the clay particles to fuse together permanently. What goes in as a soft, dusty clay object comes out as a hard, permanent ceramic piece. This process is called firing. Many ceramic pieces are fired twice — the first firing (called a bisque firing) hardens the raw clay, and the second firing (called a glaze firing) melts a glassy coating called a glaze onto the surface, giving the piece its smooth, colourful, and waterproof finish.

2. Brick-Making
The bricks used to build houses and walls are made of clay. After the clay is moulded into brick shapes and dried, the bricks are stacked inside a large kiln and fired at high temperatures. This transforms them from fragile, compressed clay blocks into the hard, durable bricks that can withstand weather, weight, and time.

3. Lime Production
Limestone (a naturally occurring rock) is loaded into a type of kiln called a lime kiln and heated intensely. This drives off carbon dioxide from the rock through a chemical reaction, producing a white powder called quicklime, which is used in construction, farming, and water treatment. Without the kiln, this chemical transformation simply cannot happen.

4. Cement Production
The cement used in concrete is made in enormous rotating cylindrical kilns called rotary kilns. Raw materials like limestone and clay are fed into one end of the slowly rotating cylinder, travel through scorching temperatures as they move toward the other end, and emerge as a material called clinker, which is then ground into the cement powder you may have seen on construction sites.

5. Drying Lumber (Wood Kilns)
Not all kilns are used for chemical transformation. A lumber kiln (also called a wood-drying kiln) uses controlled heat to remove moisture from freshly cut timber. Wet wood warps, cracks, and rots over time, so drying it in a kiln makes it stable and safe to use in construction and furniture-making. These kilns operate at much lower temperatures than ceramic or lime kilns.

6. Glass Work
Glass kilns are used to melt, fuse, or reshape glass. Artists use them to fuse pieces of coloured glass together into decorative objects, or to slump flat glass into curved moulds.
How a Kiln Works (The Basic Process)

You don't simply switch a kiln on at full blast and switch it off when you're done. The process is carefully controlled. The temperature is raised gradually to avoid cracking or shattering the objects inside. It is then held at its peak temperature for a specific period of time. Finally, the kiln is cooled down slowly — again, to prevent cracking from thermal shock (sudden temperature changes cause materials to expand or contract too quickly, which breaks them). This full process — heating up, holding, and cooling down — is called a firing cycle or simply a firing.

Kilns can be powered in different ways:

  • Electric kilns use heating elements (similar to a toaster, but far more powerful) and are common in studios and schools.
  • Gas kilns burn natural gas or propane and are widely used by professional potters and in industry.
  • Wood-fired kilns are the oldest type, still used today by traditional potters and craftspeople around the world. The ash from the burning wood can even land on pottery surfaces inside and create unique, natural glaze effects.
  • Oil-fired kilns burn fuel oil and are used in certain industrial settings.
The Key Idea to Always Remember

If you had to summarise a kiln in one sentence, it would be this:

A kiln is a purpose-built, high-temperature heating chamber used to permanently transform raw materials — most commonly clay, stone, or wood — into more durable, useful, or chemically altered forms.

It is fundamentally a tool of transformation. Whatever goes into a kiln comes out permanently and irreversibly changed. That is the essence of what a kiln is and does.

Kilter is a noun that means the proper, balanced, working condition of something — the state where everything is as it should be, functioning correctly, well-ordered, and in harmony.

Think of kilter as an invisible standard of "rightness." When something meets that standard, it is in kilter. Simple enough.

And this is crucial: you will almost never see the word "kilter" standing alone. In practice, the word is used almost exclusively in two set phrases:

  • out of kilter
  • off kilter (also written as off-kilter)

This is not unusual in English — some words only really live inside fixed phrases. "Kilter" is one of them. So learning this word means learning these phrases.

This phrase means something is not in its proper order or working condition — it is disrupted, broken, unbalanced, or not functioning the way it is supposed to.

The focus here is on something that should be working smoothly or correctly, but isn't. There is a clear expected standard, and the thing has fallen away from it.

Examples:

  • "The machine has been out of kilter since the power outage." → The machine isn't working as it should.
  • "His sleep schedule is completely out of kilter." → His sleep pattern is disrupted and irregular, when it should be regular.
  • "The trade balance between the two countries is out of kilter." → It's uneven and not as it ought to be.

Notice that "out of kilter" works for both physical things (a machine, a door hinge) and abstract things (a schedule, a relationship, an economy). This flexibility is part of why the phrase is useful.

This phrase overlaps in meaning with "out of kilter" but carries a slightly different flavor. While "out of kilter" leans toward the idea of something being broken or disrupted from a proper working state, "off kilter" often suggests something that is:

  1. Physically tilted or not straight — leaning, crooked, or misaligned.
  2. Slightly odd, unusual, or eccentric — not wrong exactly, but not quite "normal" either.

Examples:

  • "The picture frame on the wall is off kilter." → It's hanging at a slight angle; it's not straight.
  • "His sense of humor is a bit off kilter." → His humor is quirky, unusual, a little strange — but in a harmless, even charming way.
  • "After the long flight, my whole sense of time felt off kilter." → Things felt disorienting and not quite right.

With "off kilter," there is often a milder, sometimes even affectionate tone. Calling someone's humor "off kilter" is not necessarily a criticism — it can simply mean they see the world in an unconventional, unexpected way.
The Key Difference Between the Two Phrases

Out of kilterSomething has gone wrong; it's broken, disrupted, or not working. A clear sense that it needs to be fixed.
Off kilterSomething is crooked, misaligned, or quirky. Can be more neutral or even positive. Doesn't always demand a fix.

That said, in everyday usage, many people use these phrases interchangeably, and the difference is often subtle. You will not be misunderstood if you use one where the other might be slightly more precise.

It's important to understand that "kilter" does not mean chaos or extreme dysfunction. It refers to a departure from a normal, balanced baseline — not necessarily a catastrophic failure. The disruption can be minor (a slightly off picture frame) or significant (an entire economy), but the word itself is scale-neutral.

Also, "kilter" is not a negative word by itself. It only becomes negative when paired with "out of" or "off." The concept of kilter itself is neutral — it's simply the state of proper order.

Imagine a finely tuned machine running perfectly. Every gear turns at the right speed. Every part is aligned. That machine is in kilter — in its ideal condition.

Now, something goes wrong. A gear slips. Things stop meshing correctly. The machine no longer performs as it should. It is now out of kilter.

Or imagine a painting hanging straight on a wall. Someone accidentally bumps it and it tilts slightly. It is now off kilter — not broken, but not right either.

This image — of proper alignment being disrupted — is the heart of what "kilter" means, every time you see it.
9589: A kimono is a traditional Japanese garment — essentially a long, wraparound robe that has been worn in Japan for centuries. It is one of the most recognizable symbols of Japanese culture.

A kimono is a full-length robe, usually reaching all the way down to the ankles. When you lay it flat on the floor, it takes the shape of a capital letter T — with a long body and two wide, rectangular sleeves stretching out on each side.

It has no buttons, no zippers, and no hooks. Instead, the two front panels of fabric are simply crossed over each other (the left side always goes over the right side — crossing them the other way is considered disrespectful, as it is traditionally only done when dressing the deceased). The robe is then secured around the waist with a wide, decorative sash called an obi, which is tied at the back in a large, structured knot. The obi is not just functional — it is a major decorative element and can be quite elaborate.

The collar of a kimono lies flat and folded, forming a V-shape at the front of the neck.

Kimonos are traditionally made from a single long bolt of fabric — most commonly silk, cotton, linen, or synthetic materials — cut into straight rectangular pieces and stitched together. Because of this straight-cut construction, kimonos have very little tailoring or shaping; the garment gets its form from how it is wrapped and tied on the body.

Both men and women wear kimonos, though women's kimonos tend to be far more elaborate — with richer colors, more intricate patterns, longer sleeves, and more complex obi knots.

Historically, the kimono was everyday clothing in Japan. Today, however, most Japanese people wear Western-style clothing in their daily lives. Kimonos are now reserved primarily for special occasions and formal events, such as:

  • Weddings and wedding ceremonies
  • Coming-of-age ceremonies (a major celebration when a person turns 20)
  • Traditional festivals and cultural events
  • Tea ceremonies
  • New Year celebrations
  • Graduation ceremonies

At these events, wearing a kimono is a way of showing respect, honoring tradition, and marking the significance of the occasion.

Not all kimonos are the same. The style, color, pattern, sleeve length, and design of a kimono communicate specific information about the wearer — their age, gender, marital status, and the formality of the occasion. Here are the most well-known types:

Furisode — A very formal kimono worn by unmarried young women. Its most distinctive feature is its extremely long, swinging sleeves, which can reach almost to the ground. The furisode is typically worn at coming-of-age ceremonies and is brightly colored with bold, elaborate patterns.

Tomesode — A formal kimono worn by married women. Unlike the furisode, it has shorter sleeves, and its patterns are typically concentrated near the hem (the bottom edge), with the upper body kept plainer. The most formal version is black with family crests (called mon) printed on it.

Houmongi — A semi-formal kimono for women, recognizable because its pattern flows continuously across the seams of the fabric — meaning the design does not stop or break at the seams but carries on as one unified image across the whole garment.

Yukata — A lighter, more casual and informal type of kimono, typically made from cotton or synthetic fabric. It is commonly worn during summer festivals, fireworks events, and at traditional inns (called ryokan). Think of it as the relaxed, warm-weather version of a kimono.

Men's kimono — Men's kimonos are generally simpler than women's. They tend to be in darker, more subdued colors (dark blue, grey, brown, black), have shorter sleeves, and are worn with a narrow sash rather than the wide, elaborate obi of women's kimonos.

One of the most interesting things about the kimono is how much information it silently communicates. Just by looking at someone's kimono, a knowledgeable observer can often tell:

  • Age and marital status: Young unmarried women wear bright colors and long-sleeved furisode; older or married women wear more subdued colors and shorter sleeves.
  • The season: Kimonos are chosen to reflect the time of year. A kimono with cherry blossom patterns, for example, is associated with spring. Patterns featuring autumn leaves signal the fall season. Wearing a kimono whose pattern is "out of season" is considered a fashion error.
  • The occasion: The formality of the event dictates the type and color of kimono. A brightly patterned yukata at a formal wedding, for example, would be wildly inappropriate.
  • Family lineage: Formal kimonos sometimes feature small circular crests (mon) that represent the wearer's family — similar in spirit to a coat of arms.

Even the way the obi is tied, and the specific knot style chosen, can communicate information about the wearer's personality or the nature of the occasion.
The kimono in the wider world

Outside Japan, the word "kimono" is sometimes used more loosely in English to describe any loose, flowing robe or wrap garment that is styled similarly — such as a kimono robe (a lightweight, loose bathrobe with wide sleeves) or a kimono jacket (a casual, open-front cardigan-style top with wide sleeves). These items borrow the aesthetic of the traditional garment — particularly the T-shape, the wide sleeves, and the wrap-style front — but are not the traditional Japanese article of clothing itself. When used in this way, "kimono" functions as a style name rather than a reference to the culturally specific Japanese garment.

In a broader cultural sense, the kimono has become one of the most globally recognized symbols of Japan, appearing in art, fashion, film, and design worldwide. Many fashion designers around the world have drawn inspiration from its elegant silhouette and the artistry of its textiles.

A kimono is a traditional Japanese T-shaped wraparound robe, fastened with a decorative sash called an obi. It carries deep cultural significance in Japan, where different styles communicate the wearer's age, marital status, and the occasion. Once everyday clothing, it is now mainly worn for formal and ceremonial events. Outside Japan, the word is also used to describe Western garments inspired by its silhouette.
